documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: problem 1
problems.statement:
Diatoms, microscopic organisms, are an abundant food source in the oceans. They produce carbohydrates from carbon dioxide and water by photosynthesis:

$$
6\mathrm{CO_2}+6\mathrm{H_2O}+\text{solar energy}
\longrightarrow\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}+6\mathrm{O_2}.
$$

parts.statement: During their first five years, blue whales gain $75\ \mathrm{kg}$ of mass per day by feeding on krill. Each day a whale must consume ten times this mass of krill. Krill must consume $10.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ of diatoms to produce $1.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ of krill. Assume that a whale's mass gain during its first years is due to consuming carbohydrates, $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}$. Calculate the volume of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ at STP ($0\,{}^\circ\mathrm C$, $101\ \mathrm{kPa}$) that the diatoms must use to produce the carbohydrates consumed by a blue whale during its first five years.

There is $0.23\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of dissolved $\mathrm{CO_2}$ per litre of seawater, at $24\,{}^\circ\mathrm C$ and $101\ \mathrm{kPa}$.

i) If diatoms completely remove carbon dioxide from the water they process, what volume of water must they process to produce the carbohydrates required by a blue whale during its first five years?

ii) What fraction of the total ocean volume supplies the carbon dioxide for the first five years of growth of $1000$ blue whales? The ocean volume is $1.37\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m^3}$.
Three percent of the mass of a $9.1\times10^4\ \mathrm{kg}$ adult whale is nitrogen. When such a blue whale dies, what is the maximum mass of $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ available to other marine organisms?

Eighteen percent of the mass of a $9.1\times10^4\ \mathrm{kg}$ whale is carbon. Carbon returns to the atmosphere as $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and can then be removed by weathering calcium-silicate rocks:

$$
\mathrm{CaSiO_3(s)}+2\mathrm{CO_2(g)}+3\mathrm{H_2O(l)}
\longrightarrow
\mathrm{Ca^{2+}(aq)}+2\mathrm{HCO_3^-(aq)}+\mathrm{H_4SiO_4(aq)}.
$$

What is the maximum number of grams of $\mathrm{CaSiO_3}$ weathered by the carbon dioxide from the decomposition of $1000$ blue whales, the estimated annual number of deaths?

sections.statement:
i) The water volume is $4\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{dm^3}$.

ii) The fraction is $3\times10^{-5}$ of the total ocean volume ($0.03$ per mille).

$$
m(\mathrm N)=0.03\times9.1\times10^4\ \mathrm{kg}
=2.7\times10^6\ \mathrm g,
$$

$$
n(\mathrm N)=n(\mathrm{NH_4^+})
=\frac{2.7\times10^6\ \mathrm g}{14\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}}
=1.9\times10^5\ \mathrm{mol},
$$

$$
m(\mathrm{NH_4^+})
=1.9\times10^5\ \mathrm{mol}\times18\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}
=3\times10^6\ \mathrm g
=3\times10^3\ \mathrm{kg}.
$$

One whale contains $1.6\times10^4\ \mathrm{kg}$ of carbon, corresponding to $1.3\times10^6\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{CO_2}$. From the equation,

$$
n(\mathrm{CaSiO_3})=6.5\times10^5\ \mathrm{mol},
$$

$$
m(\mathrm{CaSiO_3})
=6.5\times10^5\ \mathrm{mol}\times116\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}
=7.5\times10^7\ \mathrm g.
$$

Thus $1000$ whales produce $7.5\times10^{10}\ \mathrm g$ of weathered $\mathrm{CaSiO_3}$.

problems.title: problem 2
problems.statement: Streams draining coal or metallic-ore mining areas can become acidic and contain high concentrations of dissolved iron and sulphate, because sulphur-containing ores are exposed to air or oxygenated water. The most common sulphur mineral is pyrite, $\mathrm{FeS_2}$, in which iron has oxidation state $+2$. When iron-rich streams mix with other waters, dissolved iron precipitates as goethite, $\mathrm{FeO(OH)}$. It coats the stream bottom while the water remains acidic.

parts.statement: Draw the electron-dot structure illustrating the bonding in $\mathrm{S_2^{2-}}$, showing all valence electrons.
Write a balanced equation showing how hydrogen ions are generated when pyrite is oxidized to give a solution of iron(II) and sulphate ions.
Write a balanced equation showing the additional moles of hydrogen ions generated when iron(II) ions are oxidized to goethite, $\mathrm{FeO(OH)}$.

How many moles of pyrite are required to bring $1.0\ \mathrm{dm^3}$ of pure water to pH $3.0$, if pyrite is completely converted to $\mathrm{FeO(OH)}$ and $\mathrm{H^+}$? Neglect $\mathrm{HSO_4^-}$ formation.

A stream contains $0.00835\ \mathrm M$ Fe(II). At a narrow point it enters a large pond at $20.0\ \mathrm l$ per minute. Aeration oxidizes $75\%$ of Fe(II) to Fe(III). The pond pH is above $7$, so Fe(III) immediately precipitates as $\mathrm{Fe(OH)_3}$, which becomes $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$ on ageing. What mass of $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$ is deposited in two years?

problems.title: problem 3
problems.statement:
Coniferyl alcohol, $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{12}O_3}$, is isolated from pine trees. It is insoluble in water and aqueous $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$. A solution of $\mathrm{Br_2}$ in $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ is decolorized by coniferyl alcohol, forming A, $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{12}O_3Br_2}$.

Reductive ozonolysis gives vanillin (4-hydroxy-3-methoxybenzaldehyde) and B, $\mathrm{C_2H_4O_2}$. Benzoyl chloride, $\mathrm{C_6H_5COCl}$, reacts with coniferyl alcohol in the presence of a base to give C, $\mathrm{C_{24}H_{20}O_5}$. C rapidly decolorizes aqueous $\mathrm{KMnO_4}$ and is insoluble in dilute $\mathrm{NaOH}$.

Cold HBr converts coniferyl alcohol to D, $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{11}O_2Br}$. Hot HI converts ArOR to ArOH and RI. Excess hot HI converts coniferyl alcohol to E, $\mathrm{C_9H_9O_2I}$, and $\mathrm{CH_3I}$. In aqueous base, $\mathrm{CH_3I}$ reacts with coniferyl alcohol to form F, $\mathrm{C_{11}H_{14}O_3}$. F is insoluble in strong base but decolorizes $\mathrm{Br_2/CCl_4}$ solution.

parts.statement: Draw the structures of coniferyl alcohol and A–F.

Compound A has a number of stereoisomers. Draw A and mark each chiral centre with an asterisk. Draw Fischer projections of all stereoisomers and label every chiral centre R or S to give its absolute configuration.

sections.statement:
The key states: there are no geometric isomers of A, but there are “4 diastereomers (2 pairs of enantiomers).”

problems.title: problem 4
problems.statement:
Rose oil is an essential oil obtained by steam distillation of rose plant material. It contains several terpenes, including geraniol, $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{18}O}$, A.

Oxidation of geraniol can give a ten-carbon aldehyde or ten-carbon carboxylic acid. Two moles of bromine give tetrabromide B, $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{18}OBr_4}$. Geraniol reacts with HBr to give two bromides, each $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{17}Br}$.

Vigorous oxidation of geraniol gives these three products:

![](p4-fig1)

parts.statement: Give the structure of geraniol A.
Give the structure of B.
Give the structures of the two bromides, $\mathrm{C_{10}H_{17}Br}$.
Indicate which bromide forms in greater proportions.

problems.title: problem 5
problems.statement:
Nitrogen dioxide, $\mathrm{NO_2}$, is one of the nitrogen oxides in the atmosphere. It can dimerize:

$$2\mathrm{NO_2(g)}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)}.$$

parts.statement: Show the bonds in $\mathrm{NO_2(g)}$ with a diagram, using resonance if necessary. Nitrogen dioxide is paramagnetic.
Show with bonding diagrams how two $\mathrm{NO_2(g)}$ molecules form a non-paramagnetic $\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)}$ molecule.

At $298\ \mathrm K$, the standard Gibbs energies of formation are $98.28\ \mathrm{kJ}$ for $\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)}$ and $51.84\ \mathrm{kJ}$ for $\mathrm{NO_2(g)}$. Starting with one mole of $\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)}$ at $1.0\ \mathrm{atm}$ and $298\ \mathrm K$, calculate the decomposed fraction when total pressure and temperature remain constant.
For $\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)}\rightleftharpoons2\mathrm{NO_2(g)}$, $\Delta H^\circ=58.03\ \mathrm{kJ}$. At what temperature is the decomposed fraction twice that in 5.3?

Dissociation of $\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)}$ to $\mathrm{NO_2(g)}$ is first order, with rate constant $5.3\times10^4\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at $298\ \mathrm K$. Starting at $0.10\ \mathrm M$, how many seconds are needed for $20\%$ of the original $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ to decompose?

Association of $\mathrm{NO_2(g)}$ to $\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)}$ is second order, with rate constant $9.8\times10^6\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$ at $298\ \mathrm K$. Calculate $K_c$ for $2\mathrm{NO_2(g)}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)}$.

sections.statement:
![](p5-sol-fig2)

At very low temperatures another structure, $\mathrm{O{=}N{-}ONO_2}$ (nitrosyl nitrate), is possible.

If $2(0.166)=0.332\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ decomposes, $0.664\ \mathrm{mol}$ of $\mathrm{NO_2}$ forms:

$$
K_p=\frac{(0.664/1.332)^2}{(1-0.332)/1.332}=0.496.
$$

$$
\ln\frac{K_2}{K_1}
=-\frac{\Delta H}{R}\left(\frac1{T_2}-\frac1{T_1}\right).
$$

The numerical substitution is printed with $58.03\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$:

$$
\ln\frac{0.496}{0.113}
=-\frac{58.03\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}}
{8.314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}}
\left(\frac1{T_2}-\frac1{298\ \mathrm K}\right),
$$

and the printed answer is $T_2=318\ \mathrm K$.

problems.title: problem 6
problems.statement: The atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration has increased substantially during this century and is predicted to continue increasing. The question forecasts about $440\ \mathrm{ppm}$ ($440\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{atm}$) for 2020.

parts.statement: Calculate the concentration in $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ dissolved in distilled water equilibrated with the atmosphere in 2020.
Calculate the pH of the solution in 6.1.
Calculate the enthalpy of the reaction between aqueous $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and water.
If the temperature of an equilibrated $\mathrm{CO_2}$ solution increases while the dissolved carbon dioxide concentration remains constant, will pH increase or decrease?

sections.title: Data
sections.statement:
Henry's law constant for $\mathrm{CO_2}$ at $298\ \mathrm K$: $0.0343\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,atm^{-1}}$.

Thermodynamic values at $298\ \mathrm K$, in $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$:

| Species | $\Delta_\mathrm fG^\circ$ | $\Delta_\mathrm fH^\circ$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| $\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}$ | $-386.2$ | $-412.9$ |
| $\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$ | $-237.2$ | $-285.8$ |
| $\mathrm{HCO_3^-(aq)}$ | $-587.1$ | $-691.2$ |
| $\mathrm{H^+(aq)}$ | $0.00$ | $0.00$ |

$$
\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}+\mathrm{H_2O(l)}
\longrightarrow\mathrm{H^+(aq)}+\mathrm{HCO_3^-(aq)},
\qquad\Delta G^\circ=36.3\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.
$$

$$
K=e^{-\Delta G/(RT)}=4.37\times10^{-7}.
$$

Since $x=[\mathrm{H^+}]=[\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]$,

$$
K=\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{HCO_3^-}]}{[\mathrm{CO_2}]}
=\frac{x^2}{[\mathrm{CO_2}]}.
$$

Solving gives $[\mathrm{H^+}]=2.57\times10^{-6}$ and $\mathrm{pH}=5.59$.
The reaction is endothermic, so its equilibrium constant increases with temperature. Thus $[\mathrm{H^+}]$ increases and pH decreases.

problems.statementAfterParts:
### Source notes

The historical 2020 forecast is part of the 1992 question, not a present-day atmospheric measurement. The Henry-constant unit in the question differs from the $\mathrm{M\,atm^{-1}}$ used by its key; both printed units are retained. All four connected requests and the complete data table remain one whole problem.

problems.title: problem 7
problems.statement:
After heavy spring rain, fresh-water rivers entering Chesapeake Bay reduce the salinity where oysters grow. Normal oyster growth needs a minimum chloride concentration of $8\ \mathrm{ppm}$ ($8\ \mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}$).

After one week of heavy rain, a $50.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ bay-water sample receives a few drops of $\mathrm{K_2CrO_4}$ solution and is titrated with $16.16\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.00164\ \mathrm M$ $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$. A bright red-orange precipitate forms.

parts.statement: Find the molar chloride concentration in the sample.
Is there enough chloride for normal oyster growth? Show the calculation.
Write a balanced analyte–titrant reaction equation.
Write the balanced net-ionic endpoint reaction. Which compound gives the brick-red colour?
At the endpoint $[\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}]=0.020\ \mathrm M$. Calculate the chloride concentration when the red precipitate forms.

The titration works best in neutral or slightly basic solution. Write the balanced competing reaction in acidic medium that affects the endpoint.

The sample has pH $5.10$, too acidic for accurate analysis. A buffer is normally added.

Select a buffer giving pH $7.20$ and show the calculations leading to the choice:

| System | Composition | Weak-acid $K_a$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | $0.10\ \mathrm M$ lactic acid / $0.10\ \mathrm M$ sodium lactate | $1.4\times10^{-4}$ |
| 2 | $0.10\ \mathrm M$ acetic acid / $0.10\ \mathrm M$ sodium acetate | $1.8\times10^{-5}$ |
| 3 | $0.10\ \mathrm M$ sodium dihydrogen phosphate / $0.10\ \mathrm M$ sodium hydrogen phosphate | $6.2\times10^{-8}$ |
| 4 | $0.10\ \mathrm M$ ammonium chloride / $0.10\ \mathrm M$ ammonia | $5.6\times10^{-10}$ |
For the selected system, calculate the masses of weak acid and conjugate base needed to make $500\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of stock solution buffered at pH $7.2$.

The chloride in another $50.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ sample is determined by the Volhard method. Excess $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$ is added, and excess $\mathrm{Ag^+}$ is titrated with standardized KSCN to precipitate AgSCN. Once $\mathrm{Ag^+}$ is depleted, reddish-brown $\mathrm{FeSCN^{2+}}$ signals the endpoint.

The excess silver from $50.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.00129\ \mathrm M$ $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$ requires $27.46\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $1.41\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm M$ KSCN. Calculate the sample's chloride concentration.

In water with much more chloride, gravimetric determination precipitates AgCl. AgCl undergoes photodecomposition:

$$\mathrm{AgCl(s)}\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ag(s)}+\frac12\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}.$$

With excess silver ions, a further reaction occurs:

$$
3\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}+3\mathrm{H_2O}+5\mathrm{Ag^+}
\longrightarrow5\mathrm{AgCl}+\mathrm{ClO_3^-}+6\mathrm{H^+}.
$$

If $0.010\ \mathrm g$ of a $3.000\ \mathrm g$ AgCl sample contaminated with excess silver ions undergoes these reactions, is the apparent AgCl weight too high or too low? Explain and calculate the mass difference.

Data: $K_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathrm{AgCl})=1.78\times10^{-10}$; $K_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathrm{Ag_2CrO_4})=1.00\times10^{-12}$.

sections.statement:
$$
2\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)}+\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}(aq)}
\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ag_2CrO_4(s)}\downarrow
$$

Silver chromate gives the brick-red colour.

The key prints

$$K_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathrm{Ag_2CrO_4})=[\mathrm{Ag^+}]^2[\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}]=4x^3,\quad x=[\mathrm{Ag^+}],$$

then gives $[\mathrm{Ag^+}]=7.07\times10^{-6}$ and $[\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}]=2\times10^{-2}$.

$$
[\mathrm{Cl^-}]
=\frac{K_{\mathrm{sp}}(\mathrm{AgCl})}{[\mathrm{Ag^+}]}
=\frac{1.78\times10^{-10}}{7.07\times10^{-6}}
=2.5\times10^{-5}.
$$
Maximum buffer capacity occurs when $\mathrm{pH}=\mathrm pK_a$. System 3 is best, since $\mathrm pK_a=7.2$.

$$
n(\mathrm{AgCl})_{\mathrm{lost}}
=\frac{0.010\ \mathrm g}{143.35\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}}
=6.98\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol}.
$$

$n(\mathrm{Cl_2})=\frac12(6.98\times10^{-5})=3.49\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol}$.

New AgCl is $\frac53(3.49\times10^{-5})=5.82\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol}$, equivalent to $8.34\ \mathrm{mg}$.

The silver amount equals the amount of AgCl lost:

$$
[\mathrm{Ag}]_{\mathrm{formed}}
=6.98\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mol}\times107.9\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}
=7.53\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm g.
$$

The sample mass is $3.0-0.010+0.00834+0.00753=3.006\ \mathrm g$. Thus the total solid mass (AgCl + Ag) is too high by $6\ \mathrm{mg}$.

problems.title: problem 8
problems.statement:
The Pourbaix diagrams for water, nitrogen and manganese are shown in Figure 1.

![](p8-fig1)

parts.statement:
Clear, slightly acidic well water ($\mathrm{pH}\approx5$) often deposits a black manganese solid on standing in toilet bowls.

i) Give the formula of the black solid.

ii) Give the manganese species in the water while still underground.

The diagrams indicate two nitrogen species that should oxidize $\mathrm{Mn(s)}$ to $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}(aq)}$.

i) Give their formulas.

ii) Which does not do so in practice at room temperature?

Which of these manganese forms should oxidize $\mathrm{NH_3(aq)}$ or $\mathrm{NH_4^+(aq)}$ to $\mathrm{N_2(g)}$?

$\mathrm{Mn}$, $\mathrm{Mn(OH)_2}$, $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Mn_3O_4}$, $\mathrm{Mn_2O_3}$, $\mathrm{MnO_2}$, $\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$.

Ammonium permanganate, $\mathrm{NH_4MnO_4}$, is well known; ammonium manganate, $(\mathrm{NH_4})_2\mathrm{MnO_4}$, is rarely known.

i) Is $\mathrm{NH_4MnO_4}$ expected to be thermodynamically stable? YES or NO.

ii) Is $(\mathrm{NH_4})_2\mathrm{MnO_4}$ expected to be thermodynamically stable? YES or NO.

iii) Write and balance its printed decomposition request: $\mathrm{NH_4MnO_4}$ gives $\mathrm{MnO_2}$ and $\mathrm{N_2}$.

iv) Write and balance the decomposition of $(\mathrm{NH_4})_2\mathrm{MnO_4}$ to $\mathrm{Mn}$ and $\mathrm{N_2}$.
The standard reduction potential for $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ to $\mathrm{MnO_2}$ is $E^\circ=1.692\ \mathrm V$. Use the Nernst equation to find $E$ for $0.00100\ \mathrm M$ permanganate at pH $4.0$.

sections.statement: $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ and $\mathrm{N_2}$. In practice only nitrate oxidizes Mn, because breaking the nitrogen triple bond requires very high activation energy.

i) $\mathrm{NH_4MnO_4}$: YES.

ii) $(\mathrm{NH_4})_2\mathrm{MnO_4}$: NO.

iii) $2\mathrm{NH_4MnO_4}\longrightarrow4\mathrm{H_2O}+2\mathrm{MnO_2}+\mathrm{N_2}$.

iv) $(\mathrm{NH_4})_2\mathrm{MnO_4}\longrightarrow4\mathrm{H_2O}+\mathrm{Mn}+\mathrm{N_2}$.

The diagrams indicate that Mn easily reduces $\mathrm{KNO_3}$, while the $\mathrm{MnO_2}$ potential is more positive than the nitrate potential. Thus the key says the nitrate–manganese mixture could be explosive.

problems.statement:
Pheromones are chemicals, or chemical mixtures, secreted by insects and some animals for communication. They bring about responses in other individuals of the same species.

The following pheromones undergo reactions used to determine their structures. In every case give the product structure or structures. Show geometric (cis/trans) isomers where appropriate in 9.5. Other forms of stereoisomerism may be ignored.
